newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Flabby UK oil refining sector gets reprieve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Flabby UK oil refining sector gets reprieve.

text.p: Britain's bulging oil refining industry on Friday was back to square one in its efforts to pare capacity after a proposed joint venture in south Wales fell apart.

French Elf Aquitaine and U.S. Chevron said they had abandoned plans to merge refining operations in Milford Haven, south Wales, by ceasing crude processing at the 115,000 barrels per day (bpd) Gulf Oil refinery in Pembroke. Gulf is owned by Chevron.
"The UK will still have a gasoline surplus of over four million tonnes a year, overcapacity of around 10-20 percent," said Martin Shepherdson at Edinburgh-based consultancy Wood Mackenzie.
U.S. Murphy Corp unit Murco had already announced its exit from the proposed merger, initiated last November, in favour of going it alone in the highly competitive UK petroleum retail sector.
"Following detailed studies, the two parties considered that the planned study would not provide sufficient savings in order to justify the project," Elf said in a statement.
Elf previously had said the deal could save it 50 million pounds a year.
Chevron now says it will probably attempt to sell the Milford Haven Gulf plant. If that fails it will close the refinery.
"We have always said that we do not continue to have a significant interest in the UK downstream," a company spokesman said.
But analysts said chances of a quick sale at a reasonable price looked very slim while the huge expense of dismantling a refinery and cleaning the site made closure an option of last resort.

"I really can't see who would buy it," said a London-based analyst. "No-one wants to close a refinery because of the cost. And why would you close and see your competitors' shareholders reap the benefit."

British Petroleum, which merged European refining operations with Mobil last year, has been trying for more than a year to sell its French Lavera refinery. It has ruled out closure saying it would cost about $100 million.
"This could turn into another Lavera and stretch on and on," said the London-based analyst.

A price war among gasoline retailers, initiated at the start of last year by Esso UK in response to the rapid growth of supermarkets as gasoline retailers, has hit UK retail petroleum profit margins hard.
Refining analysts say companies are battling against the tide of stagnant demand for petroleum products.
Closures and mergers would cut costs but oil refining in Europe was likely to remain a tough business in which to turn a profit, said Martin Myers at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in the U.S.
"Our view is that these changes don't change the fundamentals of the business in a significant way," said Myers. "It will remain a very competitive business."
